report.source_text: He was advised to undergo a nephrostomy for ureteral dilation followed by double J stent placement. A percutaneous approach for cyst removal was deemed very difficult in this patient, thus nephrostomy was conducted using an 8-8.9 Fr nephroscope. To be able to remove the cyst, the cyst wall had to be very thin and well-visualized to avoid renal parenchyma injury. However, in our case, the cyst wall was too thick and poorly visualized, thus cyst removal was not conducted. Cyst removal failed, thus we proceeded to perform ureteral dilatation. The double J stent was inserted and bleeding was checked. Four months after surgery, the cyst remained, but the patient was asymptomatic.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 27-year-old male presented with intermittent loin pain and partial urinary retention. Initial ultrasonography suggested pelvico ureteric junction obstruction (PUJO) with pelvicalyceal and proximal ureteric dilatation. A subsequent renal CT scan revealed a hypodense lesion in the renal pelvis, extending to the proximal ureter, measuring 5.03 × 5.36 × 5.98 cm (E002). This lesion, referred to as a cyst, was explicitly documented to be pressing on the right renal pelvic system and right proximal ureter, causing PUJO and Grade III hydronephrosis (E003). Attempts at percutaneous cyst removal failed due to a thick, poorly visualized cyst wall. The patient underwent nephrostomy for ureteral dilation and double J stent placement. Four months post-surgery, the cyst remained, but the patient was asymptomatic (E004). The final diagnosis is 'PPC-causing hydronephrosis', with 'PPC' inferred to be a parapelvic cyst based on the lesion's location and nature.
